items.feature: Object particle and polite 하다 contraction

corpusAnchor.note: 공부하다 is 공부 (studying) + 하다 (do) — 'to do studying.' Every ~하다 verb ends in 해요 in the polite form.

items.acceptableAnswerNote: Accept a natural polite answer preserving the corpus meaning and the tested feature.

items.input: I drank coffee at the cafe
items.feature: Place particle and past tense contraction
items.expectedReadingEnglish: I drank coffee at the cafe

corpusAnchor.note: Actions happen with 에서, not 에 — the cafe is the venue, not the destination. 마시다 → 마셨어요.

items.acceptableAnswerNote: Accept a natural polite answer preserving the corpus meaning and the tested feature.

items.feature: Inability negation as a free adverb

corpusAnchor.note: 못 is 안's cousin with a different meaning: not won't — CAN'T. 안 마셔요 is a choice; 못 마셔요 is ability or circumstance.

items.acceptableAnswerNote: Accept a natural polite answer preserving the corpus meaning and the tested feature.

corpusAnchor.note: 가 marks 친구 as the do-er. 'To' isn't a separate word in front — it's the particle 에 glued onto the back of 학교.
Honorifics don't just add 시 — some verbs get replaced outright. Elders don't 먹다; they 드시다.

items.feature: Topic, location noun, and existential form
items.expectedReadingEnglish: The bank is next to the hospital

corpusAnchor.note: The location frame: [thing]은/는 [landmark] [position]에 있어요. Position words are NOUNS — 병원 옆 is literally 'the hospital's side.'
